en: Then the Blessed One said: Folio 5a (G 1380; Chak 182.1–183.11;
"Subhūti, as many particles of dust as there are in the earth of this trichiliocosm great thousandfold world-system, would that be much?
He replied, "That particle of earth-dust is much, Blessed One; yet it has been called 'dustless' by the Tathāgata, and therefore it is called 'particle of earth-dust.'"
2. Thus, that which is called a "world-system" is, by the Tathāgata, declared to be a non-system; therefore it is called a "world-system."
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti? Should a Tathāgata be seen by means of the thirty-two marks of a great man?

Subhūti replied: "No, Blessed One. Why is that? Those very thirty-two marks of a great man have been described by the Tathāgata as being markless; therefore they are called the 'thirty-two marks of a great man.'"
The Blessed One said:

"Furthermore, Subhūti, if a woman or a man were to renounce as many self-existences as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā, and if another were to take up from this Dharma-discourse even a single four-line stanza— "
If one were to teach this very [teaching] to others,
on that account one would produce much merit— immeasurable and incalculable.
Then, indeed, the venerable Subhūti, through the force of the Dharma, shed tears. Wiping away his tears, he said this to the Blessed One: "It is marvelous, Blessed One;

it is most marvelous, Sugata, that this Dharma-discourse has been spoken by the Tathāgata! For from this, O Blessed One, knowledge has arisen in me such that I have never before heard this Dharma-discourse, [which is] supreme."

7. O Blessed One, those who, when this sutra is being spoken, will produce the perception of reality, will be endowed with something marvelous. And that which, O Blessed One, is the perception of reality is itself a non-perception; therefore the Tathāgata says so.
“...that there is the perception of a real entity regarding what is not a real entity—
O Blessed One, it is not surprising to me that I understand and have faith in this Dharma-discourse as it is being spoken.”
"Blessed One, those beings who shall take up this Dharma-discourse, even to the point of mastering it,
will be endowed with the most supreme wonder."
Moreover, Blessed One, the notion of a self will not arise in them;
nor the notion of a sentient being, nor the notion of a living soul, nor the notion of a person.
Why is that? Because they are free from all notions.
3. Regarding the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, the Blessed One said:
"It is so, Subhūti; those who, having heard this Dharma-discourse, shall not be terrified and shall not be utterly terrified, they will be endowed with the most supreme wonder."
They will not fall into terror.

Why is that? Subhūti, this which has been spoken of by the Tathāgata as the supreme perfection is indeed the supreme perfection; and that which the Tathāgata speaks of as the supreme perfection—[is it not so?]
Innumerable Buddhas, Blessed Ones, speak of it;
therefore it is called the "supreme perfection.
Furthermore, Subhūti, that which is the Tathāgata’s perfection of patience is itself a non-perfection.

For what reason? Subhūti, when King Kali cut the flesh from my limbs and joints, at that time I had no perception of a self, nor a perception of a being, nor a perception of a soul, nor a perception of a person. Nor did I have any perception of malice at that time. I recall, Subhūti, five hundred past births.
7. When I was the seer Kṣāntivādin, even then I had no perception of a self, no perception of a sentient being, no perception of a life-force, and no perception of a person.
Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having abandoned all perceptions, [should train...
1. By means of my flesh, all those beings will uphold awakening. For what reason? Subhūti, it is not possible for beings of inferior inclinations to hear this Dharma discourse.
It is not possible for those who hold views of a self, nor for those who hold views of a sentient being, a life-force, or a person, to hear it, to take it up, or even to master it;
such a thing is impossible.
Moreover, Subhūti, whatever spot of earth this sutra shall be proclaimed,
that spot of earth will become worthy of worship.

Subhūti, that spot of earth where those sons of good family or daughters of good family [shall dwell] will become worthy of veneration by the world with its gods, humans, and asuras; it shall be circumambulated and will become like a shrine (caityabhūta).

They will take up such sūtras as these, and even master them; they will be despised, even utterly despised. And whatever unwholesome karmas those beings committed in previous lives—which would otherwise lead to the lower realms—they will exhaust through this very state of being despised in this present life, and they shall attain the awakening of a Buddha.
I recall, Subhūti, that in the past, more than incalculable eons ago— beyond even the incalculable eons before the Tathāgata,
Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Dīpaṃkara— there were eighty-four hundred thousand nayutas of koṭis of Buddhas whom I propitiated, and having propitiated them, I did not displease them.

Furthermore, Subhūti, that which consists in my having pleased those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and not displeased them, and that which consists in their taking up these sūtras when the final period, the last five hundred years, is occurring— [these two are equal].
Subhūti,
compared to this heap of merit, that previous heap of merit does not approach even a hundredth part.
Even a thousandth part,
even a hundred-thousandth part,
even a number, even a fraction, even a calculation, even a comparison, even a likeness— none of these can express it.

3. Furthermore, Subhūti, it would not be possible [to finish describing it]. If I were to describe the mass of merit that those sons of good family and daughters of good family will acquire at that time— 4. as great as is the mass of merit those sons of good family and daughters of good family will take hold of.
Sentient beings might fall into madness or undergo mental derangement; however, Subhūti, this Dharma discourse is inconceivable, and its maturation is likewise inconceivable.
5. He asked: "Blessed One, how should one who has set out in the Bodhisattva vehicle abide, how should they practice, and how should they uplift their mind?
The Blessed One replied:
"In this regard, Subhūti, one who has set out in the Bodhisattva vehicle should generate the following thought:"

6. "All sentient beings must be led by me to final nirvana in the realm of nirvana without remainder. And yet, having thus led sentient beings to final nirvana, not a single sentient being has been led to final nirvana.
Why is that? Because...

(1) Subhūti, if the perception of a "being" (*sattva-saṃjñā*) should arise in a bodhisattva, or the perception of a "living soul" (*jīva-saṃjñā*), or the perception of a "person" (*pudgala-saṃjñā*), he is not to be called a "bodhisattva. Why is that? Subhūti, there exists no such dharma as one who has set out upon the vehicle of a bodhisattva.

"What do you think, Subhūti? Is there any dharma whatsoever which was fully awakened to as unexcelled, perfect enlightenment by the Tathāgata in the presence of the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara? He replied, "No, Blessed One, there is no such dharma whatsoever which was [fully awakened to] by the Tathāgata in the presence of the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara."
3. Having fully awakened to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment in the presence of the Tathāgata, he said:

"Therefore, I was prophesied by the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara: 'Young man, in a future time you shall become a Tathāgata named Śākyamuni, an Arhat, a perfectly enlightened Buddha. 4. For what reason? Subhūti, 'Tathāgata' is a designation for suchness (*tathatā*). Subhūti, if anyone were to say that by the Tathāgata [unexcelled...]"
"Subhūti, there is no dharma whatsoever that has been fully awakened to as unsurpassed perfect enlightenment by the Tathāgata.
Subhūti, whatever dharma has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata, therein there is neither truth nor falsehood; therefore the Tathāgata speaks."
"All dharmas are Buddha-dharmas.
Subhūti, "all dharmas" means that all of them are non-dharmas; therefore they are called "all dharmas."
"Subhūti, it is just as if there were a man who possessed a body, a great body. Subhūti said: [Folio 8b] "Who..."

1. "That person spoken of by the Tathāgata as having a body, as having a great body—that, O Blessed One, was spoken of by the Tathāgata as being bodiless; therefore he is called 'one with a body,' 'one with a great body. The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Subhūti. 2.
Any bodhisattva who should say, 'I shall bring sentient beings to final nirvāṇa'—"
He should not be called a bodhisattva. For what reason? Is there, Subhūti, any dharma whatsoever that is named "bodhisattva"?
He replied: "No indeed, Blessed One."
3. The Blessed One said:

"Therefore, the Tathāgata speaks thus: 'All phenomena are devoid of a sentient being, devoid of a life-principle, and devoid of a person. Subhūti, if a bodhisattva were to say, 'I shall bring about the array of buddha-fields,' he too would be exactly like that."
4. It should be said: for what reason? Subhūti, as for these so-called "arrays of the field," they have been described by the Tathāgata as non-arrays; therefore they are called "arrays of the field.

Subhūti, that bodhisattva who has conviction that "dharmas are selfless, dharmas are selfless"—he is designated by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, as a "bodhisattva, a bodhisattva. What do you think, Subhūti, does there exist [anything] belonging to the Tathāgata...?
The one with the fleshly eye said:
"So it is, Blessed One;
such a fleshly eye exists for the Tathāgata."
The Blessed One said:

"What do you think, Subhūti? Does the Tathāgata possess the divine eye, the wisdom-eye, the Dharma-eye, and the Buddha-eye? He replied: "So it is, Blessed One; the Tathāgata possesses them. Folio 9a (G 1386; Chak 187.14–188.7; Du 162.1–163.5).
1. The divine eye, the wisdom eye, the Dharma eye, and the Buddha eye.
The Blessed One said:

"What do you think, Subhūti? If there were as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges, and if there were as many world-systems as there are grains of sand in those [rivers], would those world-systems be numerous? The Blessed One said: [They would be.]

Subhūti, as many sentient beings as there are in those world-systems, I would know their various streams of thought. Why is that? Subhūti, "streams of thought, streams of thought" is what the Tathāgata has described as "non-streams"; therefore they are called "streams of thought. Why is that? Subhūti, a past thought is not apprehended.
A future mind is not apprehended;
a present mind is not apprehended.

What do you think, Subhūti, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to fill this great trichiliocosm with the seven precious jewels and give it as a gift, would that son or daughter of good family [thereby generate much merit]?
"Or would one generate much merit on that account?
He replied, "Much, Blessed One; much, Sugata."
The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Subhūti, so it is. On that account, that son of good family or daughter of good family would produce much merit."
If, Subhūti, there were a heap of merit, the Tathāgata would not have called it ‘a heap of merit, a heap of merit.
What do you think, Subhūti? Is the Tathāgata to be seen by means of the perfection of the form-body?

He said: "No, Blessed One. A Tathāgata is not to be seen by means of the perfection of the form-body (*rūpakāya*). Why is that? Because 'the perfection of the form-body, the perfection of the form-body'—this is a non-perfection according to the Tathāgata."
2. "That which was spoken by him is called the perfection of the form-body.
The Blessed One said: "What do you think, Subhūti? Is the Tathāgata to be perceived by means of the possession of marks? He replied:

"No, Blessed One, the Tathāgata is not to be seen by way of the perfection of marks. And why? Because that which is called the 'perfection of marks' by the Tathāgata has been taught by the Tathāgata as the 'non-perfection of marks'; therefore it is called the 'perfection of marks.
The Blessed One said:
What do you think, Subhūti? Does it ever occur to the Tathāgata to think, "I have taught the Dharma"?
Subhūti, whoever should say, "The Dharma has been taught by the Tathāgata," [would speak falsely].
Subhūti, one would be falsely accusing me by grasping at what is non-existent.
Why is that? Subhūti, regarding "the teaching of the Dharma, the teaching of the Dharma," there is no dharma whatsoever to be found that is called "the teaching of the Dharma.
Subhūti asked: "Will there be, Blessed One, any beings in the future time who [will hear] these..."
"Having heard such teachings being spoken, they will have faith in them.
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, those beings are neither beings nor non-beings. Why is that? Subhūti, 'all beings' has been spoken of by the Tathāgata as 'non-beings'; therefore they are so called."
Tib 255.3.3–4.3) 1. "All sentient beings" means:

"What do you think, Subhūti? Is there any dharma whatsoever which has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata as unexcelled, perfect enlightenment? He replied, "No, Blessed One, there is no dharma whatsoever which has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata as unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Subhūti; so it is. Not even the slightest dharma exists there, nor is it apprehended; therefore it is called 'unexcelled perfect enlightenment.
Furthermore, Subhūti, that dharma is equal; therein nothing whatsoever is unequal, and therefore it is called 'unexcelled perfect enlightenment.
That unexcelled perfect enlightenment is equal by virtue of being devoid of a life-principle (*jīva*), devoid of a sentient being (*sattva*), and devoid of a person (*pudgala*)."

4. One awakens through all wholesome dharmas. Subhūti, as for these so-called "wholesome dharmas," they have been described by the Tathāgata as being indeed non-dharmas; therefore they are called "wholesome dharmas.
Furthermore, whoever...

Furthermore, Subhūti, if someone were to collect as many heaps of the seven precious jewels as there are Sumerus, kings of mountains, in a triple-thousand great thousandfold world system and give them as a gift;

and if another were to take up even a single four-line verse from this perfection of wisdom and teach it to others— Subhūti, compared to this mass of merit, that former mass of merit does not approach even a hundredth part.
...up until near nightfall.
1. Furthermore, it is not possible.
What do you think, Subhūti? Does it ever occur to the Tathāgata to think, "I have liberated sentient beings"?
Furthermore, Subhūti, you should certainly not view it in this way.

Why is that? Because there is no sentient being whatsoever who has been liberated by the Tathāgata. If, however, Subhūti, there were any sentient being who had been liberated by the Tathāgata, that itself would constitute for him a grasping at a self, a grasping at a sentient being, and a grasping at a living soul.

3. "Subhūti, this so-called 'grasping at a self' has been taught by the Tathāgata as non-grasping; yet it is apprehended by foolish common people. Subhūti, these so-called 'foolish common people' have been taught by the Tathāgata as non-people; therefore they are called 'foolish common people. What do you think, Subhūti? Is the Tathāgata to be seen by means of the perfection of physical marks? He replied, "So it is, Blessed One; the Tathāgata is to be seen by means of the perfection of physical marks."
5. The Blessed One said:

"Furthermore, Subhūti, if a Tathāgata were to be seen by way of the perfection of his physical marks, then even a wheel-turning monarch would be a Tathāgata. Subhūti said: "As I understand the meaning of what the Blessed One has spoken..."
6. A Tathāgata is not to be seen by means of the perfection of his physical marks.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
Those who saw me by my form, those who followed me by my voice, have set out upon a false exertion.
Those people shall not see me; the Buddha is to be seen through the Dharma, for the Tathāgata is the Dharmakāya. And the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is unknowable; it cannot be known.

What do you think, Subhūti? Was supreme, perfect enlightenment realized by the Tathāgata through the possession of the marks? Indeed, Subhūti, it should not be viewed in that way; Subhūti, supreme, perfect enlightenment was not realized by the Tathāgata through the possession of the marks.
Furthermore, as for that which...

3. Subhūti, it might occur to those who have set out on the Bodhisattva vehicle that there is the designation of the destruction or annihilation of any dharma; however, Subhūti, it should certainly not be viewed in this way.

For those who have set out on the Bodhisattva vehicle, there is no designation of the destruction or annihilation of any dharma whatsoever. Furthermore, Subhūti, suppose a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to fill world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā with the seven precious jewels.
If one were to give a gift to the Tathāgatas, the Arhats, the perfectly awakened Buddhas, and if another bodhisattva were to attain patience regarding the selflessness of all phenomena,
this latter person would generate far more merit than the former.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva should not grasp at a mass of merit. Subhūti said, "Should a mass of merit not be grasped, Blessed One? The Blessed One said:
It should be embraced, Subhūti, but it should not be grasped; therefore it is said that it should be embraced.
Furthermore, Subhūti, whoever should say that the Tathāgata goes or comes,
stands or sits, or lies down—
that person does not understand the meaning of what I have spoken.
For what reason?
Subhūti, "Tathāgata" means that he has come from nowhere and gone nowhere; therefore he is called the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Furthermore, Subhūti, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family [were to give] as many [worlds] as there are in the triple-thousand great thousandfold world-system...

3. "Suppose one were to reduce the atoms of dust in a world-system to powder, making as many world-systems as there are those atoms—just like a heap of atoms. What do you think, Subhūti, would that heap of atoms be great? He replied: "4. It would be great, Blessed One; it would be a great heap of atoms. Why is that? If, Blessed One, it were a [real] heap, the Blessed One would not have called it a 'heap of atoms'."
For what reason? That which was spoken of by the Blessed One as a "collection of atoms" was spoken of by the Blessed One as "not a collection"; therefore it is called a "collection of atoms.
And that which the Tathāgata speaks of as a "trichiliocosm, a great trichiliocosm world-system," [is likewise not a world-system].
That which was spoken of by the Tathāgata as a "non-element" is called the "trichiliocosm, the great trichiliocosm world-system.
For what reason? If, Blessed One, it were an element, then, Blessed One, that would be a grasping at a whole; and that which was spoken of by the Tathāgata as a grasping at a whole—
Par 194.5–194.22; Tib 256.2.4–3.4) 1. That which was spoken by the Tathāgata as "grasping" was spoken as "non-grasping"; therefore it is called "grasping at a lump."
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, that dharma which is a grasping at a lump [of matter] is indeed beyond conventional usage and inexpressible; yet it has been grasped by foolish ordinary people.

For what reason? Subhūti, if anyone were to say thus: 'A view of self was spoken of by the Tathāgata,' or 'a view of a sentient being, a view of a soul, or a view of a person'—would that be so, Subhūti?"
"Speaking correctly, he would say:
'No, Blessed One. And why is that? Blessed One, that which is called the 'view of self' by the Tathāgata was spoken of by the Tathāgata as a non-view; therefore it is called the 'view of self.
The Blessed One said:
4. Thus, Subhūti, one who has set out on the Bodhisattva vehicle should know all phenomena and should resolve upon them in such a way that even the notion of a phenomenon does not arise.
Why is that? Subhūti, as for this so-called "notion of a phenomenon," it has been described by the Tathāgata as being no-notion; therefore it is called the "notion of a phenomenon."

Furthermore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva were to fill immeasurable and incalculable world-systems with the seven precious jewels and give them as a gift, and if a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to take up from this perfection of wisdom even a single four-line verse, and should preserve, teach, and master it—[the latter would generate a greater merit].
Tib 256.3.4–3.8) 1. He would generate even more merit than that—immeasurable and incalculable.
And he would proclaim it in such a way that he does not proclaim it; therefore it is said, "he would proclaim it."
A star, a visual impairment, a lamp, a mirage, a dewdrop, a bubble, a dream, lightning, and a cloud— thus should the conditioned be viewed.

The Blessed One having spoken thus, the elder Subhūti, with a joyful mind, as well as those monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen, and the world with its gods, humans, asuras, and gandharvas, rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said.
The Diamond-Cutter Prajñāpāramitā is completed.
